newsitem.title: IRAQ: Iraq prices plunge after oil deal.
newsitem.headline: Iraq prices plunge after oil deal.

text.p: Food prices plunged on Tuesday in the wake of Iraq's oil-for-food deal with the United Nations but shoppers delayed purchases in expectation of further falls.
Mountains of sugar, rice and flour blocked shop entrances in Jamila district of Baghdad as Iraqi traders tried to empty warehouses. But the goods, so dear and scarce on Monday, had no buyers.
With prices already falling sharply following announcement of the limited oil sale agreement on Monday, shoppers and retailers said they preferred to cling to their dinars, which are rising in value.
Iraq's dinar currency soared to 1,100 against the U.S. dollar from 1,650 and money changers said they expected it to strengthen further once formal approval is given for Iraqi oil exports to begin.
Iraq's acceptance of all U.N. conditions, which had obstructed implementation of the oil-for-food deal, brought cheers from Iraqi women in Jamila, Baghdad's commercial food centre.
The news was not so pleasant for food traders, who pay for imports in dollars. "It is the second big loss in less than a year. I could go bust this time," said a flour merchant.
A 50 kg (110 lb) sack of flour, worth 26,000 dinars on Monday was offered for less than 18,000 on Tuesday. There were no buyers.

A 15 kg (33 lb) tin of cooking oil slumped to 10,000 dinars from 20,000. Rice, Iraq's staple, dropped to 325 dinars a kg (2.2 lb) from about 700. A kilogram (2.2 lb) of sugar, in acute shortage in Baghdad, fell to 470 dinars from 800.
Young boys and girls drove empty carts on Jamila's pavements. "If I buy a sack of sugar at 22,000 dinars now who can guarantee it will not drop further later in the day," said Usman Yousif, 17.
Women vendors sat on the ground on an open space opposite wholesalers venting their anger at what they described as Baghdad's "fat cats."
The women used to buy from traders at a discount and carry sacks of sugar, flour or rice on their heads to sell per kilo to government civil servants and other low income groups.
Shoppers, curious to see the falling prices, crammed Jamila on Tuesday and it was difficult for cars to make their way into the two lane street.
"I am not going to buy because I am not afraid prices will rise again. They will fall more and more. It is serious this time," said Ali Salem.
It was the second sudden surge in the value of the Iraqi dinar -- and a corresponding plunge in prices -- in less than a year.
In January, when Iraq agreed to talks with the United Nations on its oil-for-food offer the dinar soared as high as 450 to the dollar.

The plan, signed in May, is outside U.N. trade sanctions imposed for Iraq's 1990 invasion of Kuwait. It lets Baghdad export $2 billion of oil in each six-month period to buy food and medical supplies.

The deal would allow exports of 700,000 to 800,000 barrels per day at current prices, compared to more than 2.5 million a day before sanctions. The sale of oil and purchase of supplies will be under U.N. monitoring.
